findings.text: Partition CPU accounting distinguishes CPUs logically added to a child from those removed, each derived as an intersection with the parent effective set. A housekeeping compatibility check applies when a valid partition observes a parent state change, with direction depending on whether the parent is a root or isolated partition. CPUs taken from the parent must be active and remain within the parent effective set. When the parent would be left without CPUs while still hosting tasks, the operation is reported as a no-CPU error and removal is suppressed in favour of a revised addition.

Partition validity follows a sign-negation discipline for the update command: a valid root or isolated state becomes its invalid counterpart when an error is recorded, and an invalid state becomes its valid counterpart when no error remains. The error is stored once in the partition error field. If neither addition nor removal is required and the state is unchanged the operation succeeds without further effects. Changes to the exclusivity attribute are deferred past validation for the update command and applied at commit or after unlock depending on command.

Sibling exclusivity revalidation scans child partitions under read-side protection, skipping the subject itself, and only permits an invalid-to-valid transition when no sibling conflicts; otherwise a non-exclusive error is recorded. Commitment of the new partition state together with parent effective adjustments is serialized by an interrupt-disabled callback spin lock, with task mask refresh, sibling refresh, load-balance refresh and change notification performed outside or after that critical section.

Effective CPU computation for a partition first refreshes the exclusive set and restricts it to active CPUs, then examines each valid child. A child whose effective exclusive set is not contained in the parent exclusive set is marked with an invalid-CPU error, as is a child that would exhaust the parent set while the parent remains populated. Erroneous children are invalidated under the callback lock and notified, while healthy children have their exclusive CPUs subtracted from the new effective set. A remote child beneath a partition is treated as unexpected.

A CPU list string is accepted only when it parses and denotes a subset of the top-level allowed set. Partition validation accepts members unconditionally, rejects empty effective exclusive sets as invalid CPUs, rejects housekeeping conflicts, and rejects configurations that would starve parent tasks of CPUs, in that conceptual precedence.

CPU-driven partition maintenance is a no-op for members. Otherwise validation outcome is recorded in both live and trial state, then remote partitions follow a remote disable or remote update path while local partitions follow an invalidate or update path on the parent effective mask.

Changing the allowed CPU set is a no-op when the new set equals the current set. Otherwise a trial exclusive set is derived, the change is validated before temporary mask allocation, and hierarchy-wide propagation is forced when the effective exclusive set differs. Partition maintenance runs before commit, then allowed and effective exclusive sets are installed atomically under lock with partition data reset on loss of validity, followed by hierarchical refresh and scheduling domain maintenance.

Changing the exclusive CPU set mirrors the allowed-set flow but additionally rejects sibling exclusive overlaps. Trial derivation reports conflict as an error without validation. Commit installs exclusive and effective exclusive sets under lock with the same validity-loss reset, and hierarchical refresh occurs only when the result is a valid partition or the effective set changed, followed by scheduling maintenance when a partition state is present.
The migration work object aggregates four members: a queueable work item, a memory descriptor pointer, a source node mask and a destination node mask describing the requested move.

The migration handler retrieves its enclosing work object from the queued work item, migrates all pages of the stored descriptor between the stored node masks without regard to the worker own allowed nodes, then releases the descriptor and the work object. A separate flush handler drains the dedicated migration workqueue and frees its callback. Scheduling allocates a callback, arms it as task work for resume-time execution on the current task, and frees it when allocation or enqueue fails.
Task work queuing is available as a cross-file interface that attaches a callback to a chosen task with a selectable notification mode and reports success or failure.
A query entry reports whether the current task cpuset pointer equals the global rebound marker, evaluated under read-side protection.

Enqueue fails when the target has exited and rejects non-current targets or builds without interrupt-work support for non-maskable notification. Auxiliary stack recording is skipped for that mode. Notification behaviour is selected by mode: silent, resume notification, signal with inter-processor signalling, signal without it, or resume flag plus interrupt work queueing. Unknown modes trigger a one-time warning but still succeed in queueing.

The per-task work list is updated with a lock-free compare-and-exchange retry loop that links the new callback at the head, observing a dedicated exited sentinel to detect dead targets via a single atomic read.

Memory node refresh walks descendants in pre-order under read-side protection, recomputing each effective mask from its parent. Subtrees whose mask is unchanged are skipped via the rightmost descendant. Online references are taken before dropping read protection, the new mask is installed under the callback lock, a version-specific equality expectation between allowed and effective masks is checked, and per-cpuset task node masks are refreshed.

Changing the allowed node set requires successful list parsing and containment within the top-level allowed set, with unchanged values returning early. Validation precedes insane-configuration normalization, then the new allowed set is installed under lock and used as scratch for hierarchical effective-mask refresh.

Partition state changes from member require a non-empty exclusive set and absence of remote overlap when the parent is the top set, enabling locally when the parent is a valid partition and remotely otherwise. Transitions between active states only alter isolation and load balance, gated by isolated-CPU update permission and housekeeping compatibility. Return to member is always permitted and defers child invalidation. Errors negate the requested state, update exclusivity accordingly, and on commit either reset partition data or update isolated CPUs, followed by forced hierarchy refresh on demotion, scheduling refresh, notification and optional domain rebuild.

Task attachment is refused when the destination lacks effective CPUs or, outside version two, lacks allowed memory. Source and destination cpusets are queued once into global attach lists and global change flags record CPU or memory differences. Scheduling permission is required except in version two when nothing changed and in version one when the source was already empty. Deadline bandwidth reservation selects an active CPU within each requesting destination and allocates its accumulated bandwidth, failing when none exists. Clearing the attach lists re-arms nodes and either accounts migrated deadline tasks or releases reserved bandwidth on cancellation.

One-time warnings guard unexpected states: removed CPUs not remaining within the parent effective set, a remote partition appearing beneath another partition root, and a newly created valid partition with an empty effective exclusive set.

Negative error signalling uses standard codes: invalid argument for unparsable or non-subset lists, sibling conflicts, missing active CPU selection and misuse of non-maskable notification; no space when the destination cannot host tasks; out of memory for temporary mask allocation failures; no such process when queueing work on an exited task.

Interrupt-disabled callback spin locking serializes installation of CPU allowed, exclusive, effective and node-mask state together with partition state and error publication, while read-side protection covers child, descendant and current-cpuset traversals, with hierarchy walks acquiring online references before releasing read protection and then taking the spin lock.
A file-private global pointer identifies the cpuset currently undergoing memory rebound and is consulted by the rebound query.
